hook_text: Hold a square of polyester over a candle and watch it melt into a bead. Now imagine that bead on skin. That is why fire fighters never wear it.
clip_script: Start with the danger. A fire fighter faces flame, radiant heat and steam. An NSRI volunteer faces cold sea, waves and dark. Each danger asks for a property: flame resistance, insulation, waterproofing, buoyancy, visibility. Now the fibres. Cotton soaks and burns. Wool warms even wet and chars slowly. Polyester and nylon are tough and dry fast but melt. Aramids char and never melt. Make them into fabric: weave for strength, knit for stretch, coat with PVC to keep rain out, laminate a membrane to let sweat out. Then stack them. Fire jacket: aramid shell, steam barrier, air-trapping liner. Sea rescue: wicking base, fleece, coated outer with sealed seams, a bright life jacket with reflective tape. No single fabric does it all. Layers do.
visual_style: Whiteboard two-column hazard and property table; swatches with water drop, tear and flame results; a jacket cross-section with three labelled layers.
mood: Respectful and investigative, taking gear apart.
pacing: Danger, property, fibres, fabrics, layers, each a few seconds.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and work out the layers in a jacket you own.
